title: New-build gypsum, Leesburg basements, and why Ashburn returns fill faster than they should
headline: New-build gypsum, Leesburg basements, and why Ashburn returns fill faster than they should
description: Loudoun County's mix of historic Leesburg homes and active Ashburn development creates two distinct duct challenges. Learn the difference — and how to address each.

sections.heading: Leesburg and Ashburn share a county, not a duct problem
paragraphs: Drive through Leesburg's historic district and the houses are brick colonials and frame farmhouses with basements that predate air conditioning. Drive ten miles southeast to Ashburn, Broadlands, or Brambleton and the homes are vinyl-and-composite construction less than fifteen years old, built on slabs or shallow crawlspaces with high-efficiency HVAC from day one.

Both housing types develop duct contamination, but the mechanism is different. Leesburg homes accumulate moisture-bonded organic debris over decades. Ashburn homes arrive with construction-phase mineral dust embedded in the trunk walls from the first week the system ran. A county-wide blog post that treats both the same way misses the point, so this article addresses each pattern separately.

sections.heading: Leesburg basements and the slow accumulation pattern
paragraphs: Older Leesburg homes have full basements where stone or block walls absorb and release ground moisture in a seasonal rhythm. The air handler and trunk lines run through that space, staying cool in summer and cold in winter. During the humid months, supply trunks regularly drop below the dew point. Condensation forms. Pollen from Loudoun's remaining farmland tree lines and residential street plantings sticks to the wet surface.

This is a slow-moving problem. One season of condensation is trivial. Ten or twenty seasons of it produce a layered deposit that restricts airflow and supports microbial growth in the absence of light and air movement. The house looks and feels fine until someone lifts a register and sees the inside of the trunk for the first time.

sections.heading: Ashburn and Brambleton: what the data-center corridor leaves behind
paragraphs: Loudoun County hosts the densest concentration of data centers in the world, and the construction required to build them — along with the residential subdivisions that house the workers — keeps heavy earthmoving equipment and drywall crews active year-round. Fine particulate from those sites drifts downwind across occupied neighborhoods.

On top of the ambient construction dust, each new home's own HVAC system was loaded during the build phase. Gypsum fines, joint compound dust, and insulation fibers deposited on trunk walls before the first owner changed the first filter. Unlike organic debris, these mineral particles do not break down. They form a hard film that airflow alone does not dislodge, and they persist until mechanically removed.

sections.heading: Recognizing the Loudoun-specific pattern
paragraphs: The two Loudoun duct problems leave different calling cards. Moisture-based buildup in a Leesburg basement announces itself through smell. Construction-phase contamination in an Ashburn home announces itself through dust. Some homeowners have both — particularly those in Leesburg's newer infill subdivisions where renovation and proximity to active lots combine the two mechanisms:
listItems: Leesburg pattern: a damp, cellar-like odor from lower-level registers each time the AC starts, fading once continuous operation dries the trunk surfaces.
Ashburn pattern: a persistent pale dust on dark surfaces near supply vents, returning days after cleaning even with windows closed and a fresh filter installed.
Combined pattern: both the smell and the dust, common in recently renovated older homes or new construction adjacent to an active Leesburg infill site.

sections.heading: Addressing the county's dual duct challenges
paragraphs: Leesburg moisture homes benefit from a dehumidifier and periodic duct cleaning timed to the end of the humid season. Ashburn construction homes benefit from a single thorough post-occupancy cleaning followed by standard maintenance intervals. Either scenario starts with a professional assessment that determines what the trunk walls are holding and how much airflow the buildup has compromised.

Flat-rate scheduling for all Loudoun communities is on the [Loudoun County service page](/locations/loudoun). Stacked townhomes in Ashburn and Brambleton should pair duct work with [dryer vent cleaning](/dryer-vent-cleaning) — long vent runs in three-story construction commonly trap lint at bends that are inaccessible from either end without professional equipment.

faq.q: When should Loudoun homeowners consider duct cleaning?
faq.a: After nearby build-out or renovations that put fines in returns — or when Loudoun registers refilm within days of wiping.
